articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian 'Shadow Banking' Network Facilitating Billions in Illicit Transactions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on a vast Iranian 'shadow banking' network, comprising eight individuals and 22 entities across Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, and Hong Kong. This action is part of Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at disrupting Iran's illicit financial activities.

The designated network is accused of facilitating billions of dollars in transactions outside established sanctions controls, providing a critical financial lifeline for the Iranian regime. The Treasury Department highlighted that these networks assist Iranian-linked organizations in obtaining foreign currency and conducting international transactions.

The designations were issued under Executive Order 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, and Executive Order 13224, the U.S. counterterrorism sanctions authority. This move underscores an ongoing effort by the U.S. to curb Iran's ability to generate revenue and fund its destabilizing activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Iranian Oil Facilitators, Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated four Iranian individuals for their involvement in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting previously sanctioned entities, as part of Operation Economic Outcast. The individuals, Mojtaba Arabnejad, Mohammad Javad Bavand, Mohammadhossein Servati, and Majid Taj, are accused of exploiting Iran's oil sector for personal gain.

Concurrently, OFAC issued two new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 1277 and 1278). These FAQs clarify that OFAC's sanctions authority covering Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors does not automatically sanction all persons operating in those sectors.

The guidance also confirms that authorized activities involving Cuba's marine sector, including payments to Cuban ports for authorized trade and certain humanitarian transactions, may continue. The Iran designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order 13902 and Executive Order 13224, as amended.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Illicit Drugs General License, Amends Russia-Related GL, and Designates Narcotics and Cyber Actors
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit drug trafficking networks and malicious cyber operations.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, authorizing the wind-down of transactions involving certain persons blocked on November 19, 2026. This license provides a limited period for legitimate parties to cease dealings with the newly sanctioned entities.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License 131L, which authorizes certain transactions related to negotiating and entering into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with related maintenance activities. Associated Russia-related FAQs 1224 and 1225 were also amended.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Hizballah Charity and Gold Smuggling Network in Counter Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated a Lebanon-based charity, its founder, and members of a Lebanon- and Türkiye-based gold and cash smuggling network for supporting Hizballah. This action, taken under counterterrorism authority Executive Order 13224, aims to disrupt Hizballah's use of charitable organizations and illicit financial networks to raise and move funds.

The designated charity, Wa Ta'awanu Association, and its founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, are accused of supporting Hizballah under the guise of humanitarian assistance. OFAC alleges that Wa Ta'awanu channels donor funds towards Hizballah's activities and provides a pretext for their operations in southern Lebanon.

The action also targets a gold and cash network tied to Hizballah and Iran's IRGC-Qods Force, highlighting the use of cross-border couriers and gold trading companies to move illicit funds. This is part of Treasury's ongoing Operation Economic Outcast.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations Supporting Mexican Cartels
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated two Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations, Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization, for their involvement in illicit narcotics activities and support for Mexican narco-terrorist cartels. This action was taken under counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities.

Los Lorenzanas was also designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the State Department. OFAC updated the listing of Los Huistas Drug Trafficking Organization to include secondary sanctions risk and links to the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación.

These designations expose the groups to asset freezes and prohibit U.S. persons from dealing with them, with secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886, and Executive Order 14059.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran-Related SDN Listing for Volta Shipping Services
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has updated the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List entry for Volta Shipping Services LLC, a UAE-based company linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. The update changes the company's listed alias from Volta Shipping Services FZCO to Volta Container Line FZCO.

The company remains designated under Executive Order 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, and continues to be subject to secondary sanctions risk. This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the accuracy and effectiveness of its sanctions lists.
This administrative update ensures that financial institutions and other entities can accurately identify and comply with sanctions related to this entity.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Canada-Based Money Services Businesses Tied to Iran
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned eight Canada-based money services businesses for facilitating transactions involving Iran. This action, part of Operation Economic Outcast, targets international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions.

These businesses are accused of converting Iranian currency into digital assets and conducting transactions with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The action was coordinated with FinCEN and Canada's FINTRAC and was taken under Executive Order 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy. This highlights the ongoing focus on disrupting Iran's access to the global financial system through various means, including digital assets.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. This action aims to combat malicious cyber activities and disrupt the financial networks of criminal enterprises.
In addition to these designations, OFAC published a Cuba-related Determination. This determination provides further guidance and clarity regarding U.S. sanctions policy concerning Cuba.

These actions underscore OFAC's commitment to protecting the U.S. financial system from illicit activities, whether they originate from cyber threats or transnational criminal networks, while also refining existing sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on the Iranian regime.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, providing guidance and warnings to the public regarding potential sanctions risks.
Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question, offering updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.' This license facilitates the orderly cessation of certain financial activities.

This amended general license provides a specific timeframe for the wind-down of transactions, ensuring that parties can comply with U.S. sanctions while minimizing disruption to legitimate business operations.

The issuance of General License FF-1 follows a pattern of OFAC providing clear guidance for the termination of activities with sanctioned entities, emphasizing the importance of a structured approach to sanctions compliance.

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced an enforcement action against Flagstar Bank, N.A., Hicksville, New York, assessing a civil money penalty of $112,000. The penalty was imposed for a pattern or practice of violating the Flood Disaster Protection Act.

The OCC utilizes enforcement actions to ensure that bank boards of directors and management take timely corrective measures for identified deficient practices or violations. This action underscores the OCC's commitment to enforcing compliance with federal banking laws and regulations.

In addition to this penalty, the OCC also announced the termination of a cease and desist order against USAA Federal Savings Bank, Phoenix, Arizona, dated December 18, 2024, indicating that the bank has achieved substantial compliance with the previous enforcement action.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Joint Statement on BSA Reporting in Response to Service Disruption
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), along with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the National Credit Union Administration, has issued a joint statement of supervisory policy. This statement addresses a service disruption adversely impacting financial institutions' ability to satisfy Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) reporting requirements.

The joint statement provides that supervised financial institutions will not be subject to supervisory or enforcement actions related to BSA reporting requirements as a result of the ongoing service disruption, subject to certain conditions and limitations. This relief supports similar guidance issued by FinCEN on November 24, 2026.

The service disruption specifically affects financial institutions that, as of November 18, 2026, used Secure Data Transfer Mode (SDTM) to submit BSA reports. This coordinated response aims to mitigate the impact of the disruption on financial institutions' compliance obligations.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities to Entity List Over Advanced Computing Diversion Risk
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List, effective November 23, 2026. These entities, located in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand, have been identified as posing a significant risk of diverting advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.

The additions include three entities in Malaysia, three in Singapore, and one in Thailand. For each listed entity, a license is now required for all items subject to the EAR, and license applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.

A savings clause allows certain shipments already en route aboard a carrier on November 23, 2026, to proceed to their destination under previous eligibility, provided the export, reexport, or transfer is completed by December 23, 2026. This action underscores BIS's commitment to preventing the circumvention of U.S. export controls on sensitive technologies.

articles.headline: BIS Issues Interim Final Rule Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published an interim final rule (IFR) on November 19, 2026, to address concerns regarding remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers. This rule is designed to prevent the circumvention of existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.

The IFR introduces a new end-use control, requiring a license when an exporter knows that covered items will be sent to a data center, anywhere, that provides more than 12,000,000 aggregate TPP (Total Processing Power) to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau.

This regulatory change also formalizes the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which BIS announced in May 2025. The move reflects an ongoing effort by the U.S. government to close gaps in its chip controls and enforce restrictions on advanced computing technologies.

articles.headline: Additions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding 7 entities to the Entity List, under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
